name: Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions
subtitle: A cultural property on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1979.

parts.text: UNESCO describes the property in these words: “The remains of fortified trading-posts, erected between 1482 and 1786, can still be seen along the coast of Ghana between Keta and Beyin. They were links in the trade routes established by the Portuguese in many areas of the world during their era of great maritime exploration.”
The property is a group of forts and castles along the coast. Cape Coast Castle is one of them, and a 2022 newspaper feature gives its building history.
It says the Portuguese had a trade lodge there in 1555, and that the Swedes began the permanent structure in 1653.
Dutch occupation began in 1660. A British fleet under Captain Holmes took the fort in 1665, and by 1700 the British had upgraded it into a castle.
After a French naval bombardment left it badly damaged, the English rebuilt it entirely after 1760. The feature adds that in the 18th century it became the centre of European education in Ghana.
The feature mentions the castle's part in the trans-Atlantic slave trade but does not describe it.

gaps: The other forts in the property, which this card does not describe (Elmina is the best known).
The slave trade at the castle: numbers, conditions, and how the site tells that history today. The only source read here does not cover it.
A scholarly history to check the dates of changes of control, which differ between sources.
